title: Beads from Shiva's tears
hookLine: Shiva opens his eyes after a long meditation, and his tears become the seeds of a mala
carry: all things strung on God, like mala beads

cards: In the Shiva Purana, Shiva sits in meditation for a thousand years of the gods. When at last he opens his eyes, tears fall from them to the earth.
Where they land, trees grow, and their seeds are called rudraksha: Rudra's eye, Rudra being a name of Shiva. Dark, knobbly seeds, with lines running down their sides.
Devotees of Shiva string them into a mala, and many wear one, or count a mantra on it, every day.

teach.b: Mala means a garland, the same word as flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting a mantra.
Devotees of Shiva favor rudraksha; devotees of Vishnu and Krishna favor tulsi wood, from the holy basil many families tend at home.

teach.h: THE MERU: THE BEAD YOU DON'T CROSS.
teach.b: One bead is larger and sits apart, with a tassel: the meru, sharing its name with the sacred mountain at the center of the world.

Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it; at the end of a round, you turn the string and go back. Their reasons vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru or for God, and you don't step over what you honor.
Others say turning back keeps each round awake. Now the teaching the beads carry.
In the Gita's seventh chapter, Krishna says all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see; the thread holding them is hidden.
That's a central Hindu teaching: the many things of the world aren't scattered. One divine reality runs through them all, the way one cord runs through every bead.
And in the sixth chapter Krishna says, wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back.

teach.h: EACH BEAD, A RETURN TO THE THREAD.
teach.b: The bead is that return, made into something your thumb can feel. The mind drifts to a bill or a text; the thumb moves to the next bead; you're back on the thread.
Shiva's seeds or Vishnu's basil, the mala teaches with your hands: many beads, one thread.

how: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.

o: a lucky charm worn to keep bad luck away
a counting game played with beads at a fair
many beads on one hidden thread, as the world is strung on God

games.q: the mala in the hand — tap the pairs.
p: holy basil, loved by Vishnu's devotees
the larger bead you don't cross
the world strung on Krishna like gems

s: at the meru bead, you keep going round in the same direction
teachers in several lineages say to turn the string around and go back rather than cross it.
in the Shiva Purana, rudraksha trees grow from Shiva's tears
the tears fell when he opened his eyes after a long meditation.
a mala is mainly a lucky charm
it's a garland for counting japa; its hidden thread pictures the God on whom all things are strung.

games.q: halfway through a round of japa, you realize your mind has wandered for ten beads. what does the mala teach you to do?
o: move to the next bead and come back; you never left the thread.
start the whole round over, since those ten didn't count.
stop for the day; a wandering mind spoils japa.
games.why: Krishna says to bring the wandering mind back, and that all things are strung on him like gems on a thread. the next bead is the return.

practice: Hold a mala if you have one, or touch the thumb to each fingertip in turn, saying your mantra once with each touch, silently or in a whisper; Om will do, or a word from your own tradition.
When the mind drifts, don't scold it; let the next touch be the coming back. At the end of a round, pause, turn around, and go back the other way.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and the one thread running through every bead.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: rudraksha, Rudra's eye, the seed the Shiva Purana says grew from Shiva's tears.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: all things strung on God, like mala beads. Each bead brings you back to the thread. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Vidyeshvara Samhita 25 (the origin of rudraksha)
